speaker: Doctor
text: Good morning, I am Dr. Agent. I understand you are experiencing double vision, difficulty climbing stairs, and weakness in your upper limbs; could you tell me when these symptoms first started and if they have been getting worse?

speaker: Patient
text: The double vision usually happens when I look up or down, and the weakness in my arms and legs gets worse after activity but improves if I rest. I have not noticed balance problems or numbness.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for that detail; the fluctuation of symptoms with activity and rest is a key clue. To narrow this down, does the double vision ever resolve when you close one eye? Also, have you noticed any difficulty with chewing or swallowing recently?

speaker: Patient
text: I have not had recent infections or fevers, and there is no family history of neurological disease. The weakness feels symmetrical in both arms and legs.

speaker: Doctor
text: The symptoms of fluctuating weakness worsening with activity and the specific nature of your double vision are very suggestive; does covering one eye completely eliminate the double vision? Additionally, have you noticed any drooping of your eyelids or a "heavy" feeling in your eyes?

speaker: Patient
text: I have not had trouble swallowing or slurred speech. I also have not noticed breathing difficulty, and the symptoms started gradually about a month ago.

speaker: Doctor
text:
That is good to know; the absence of bulbar symptoms and breathing issues helps narrow the differential. Given the fluctuating weakness that worsens with activity and your specific double vision, could you describe your eye movements? Do you have any trouble looking up at the top of a door frame or down at your feet? Also, is there any family history of similar symptoms?

DIAGNOSIS READY: Myasthenia Gravis

The presence of anti-AChR antibodies, combined with your fluctuating muscle weakness that worsens with activity and improves with rest, along with the specific nature of your double vision, confirms the diagnosis of Myasthenia Gravis. The decreased response on nerve stimulation further supports this neuromuscular junction disorder.
